proposal.name: cloud_form
proposal.question: Which of these was it most like?

values.label: thin streaks or brush strokes, like combed hair
a layer broken up into many repeated lumps, rolls or ripples
a few small separate puffs or tufts, with sky between them
smooth and featureless - a sheet, veil or solid slab
a single smooth almond or lens
one long horizontal tube or roll
a puffy heap or tower, bulging on top
torn ragged shreds with no definite shape

proposal.rationale: Drops the overlapping tufts/rolls/flat_patches split that caused most shape errors: castellanus clouds go to patterned_layer (as 80-93% of experts answered) and floccus to separate_tufts, so the two are cleanly told apart.

proposal.name: lump_size
proposal.question: If it was patterned with repeated lumps or ripples, how wide was one of them, measured against your hand held at arm's length?

values.label: no repeated pattern - it was smooth, streaky, or one single cloud
smaller than your little fingernail - grains or fine ripples
about one to three fingers wide
wider than your whole fist

proposal.rationale: The size of a repeated element is the one height cue an untrained eye can measure, but the old version invited people to call a whole cumulus a 'large lump'; restricting it to repeated patterns kills the none/large confusion while keeping the cirrocumulus/altocumulus/stratocumulus ladder.

why: 3 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: heap_proportions
proposal.question: If it stood up as a heap or tower on its own, how tall was it compared with how wide?

values.label: it was not a heap or tower at all - a layer, sheet, streaks or a pattern of lumps
clearly wider than tall - a low bun
about as tall as it was wide
clearly taller than wide - a tower

proposal.rationale: The old 'none' option lost to 'flat' 46 times because a layer really is much wider than tall; naming the escape option 'not a heap at all' removes the overlap and leaves a clean three-step scale for the cumulus family.

why: 3 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: brightness
proposal.question: How bright or dark did it look?

values.label: white or pale - no part of it really dark
plainly grey, like wet pavement
dark grey to nearly black, making the day gloomy

proposal.rationale: Same three steps, but with the assignments the experts actually gave: congestus, cumulus fractus and stratocumulus floccus read white, altostratus opacus reads plain grey, so only the genuinely gloomy clouds sit in 'dark'.

why: 5 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: sun_view
proposal.question: What did the sun (or moon) look like where this cloud passed in front of it?

values.label: a ring of light circling it (choose this if there was a ring, even though the sun showed too)
the sun's disc still sharp-edged, no ring
a pale bright blur - you could tell where the sun was, but not its edge
no sign of the sun through it at all
the sun was nowhere near this cloud, or out of sight

proposal.rationale: Folds the halo question into the sun question and adds an explicit 'sun not in view' option, so the 74%/80% skip rates become usable answers; it also carries the classic distinction that the sun's outline shows through stratus but only as ground glass through altostratus.

why: 1 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: sky_behind
proposal.question: What was behind and above it?

values.label: open blue sky (or stars) behind it
another, bigger cloud mass behind or above it
nothing behind it - this cloud covered the whole sky itself

proposal.rationale: Replaces the near-unanswerable halo question with something visible in every photo, and it is the one cue that pins down scud (stratus fractus, always under a bigger deck) and the squall roll cloud, which is backed by its storm.

why: 1 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: underside_edge
proposal.question: What was the bottom of it like?

values.label: a definite bottom, flat and level, like a lid
a definite bottom, but torn, tattered or hanging in wisps
no bottom edge to see - it faded away or you simply could not make one out

proposal.rationale: Merges the old 'undefined' and 'not visible' options, which people could not tell apart (67 of 148 answers landed on 'undefined' regardless of truth), leaving three states an ordinary observer can actually distinguish.

why: 5 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: lump_shading
proposal.question: Did its lumps have grey shaded undersides?

values.label: there were no lumps - it was smooth, streaky or one plain cloud
lumpy, and the lumps were white all over with no grey undersides
lumpy, and the lumps were clearly darker underneath

proposal.rationale: As a yes/no it forced an answer about lumps on clouds that have none, which is why 20 of 53 'yes' clouds were answered 'no'; a third option for lumpless cloud makes the remaining split (cirrocumulus white versus altocumulus and stratocumulus shaded) a reliable height cue.

why: 6 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: falling_visible
proposal.question: Could you see anything falling out of it?

values.label: nothing at all
streaks hanging below it that faded out well above the ground
grey shafts reaching the ground under part of it
rain or snow out of the whole layer, blurring the view in every direction
lightning, thunder or hail

proposal.rationale: Reworded so each option describes something visible in the sky rather than the weather over time, which cuts the recall-from-memory answering flagged in the leakage check; the fine trails of cirrocumulus and stratocumulus floccus are moved to 'nothing', matching the 73-80% of experts who saw none.

proposal.name: trailing_tails
proposal.question: Did it trail fibres or tails, as if its edges were being combed out sideways?

values.label: yes - hairy, streaky, drawn-out edges
no - its edges were rounded or sharply cut

proposal.rationale: Mamma earned 0.01 bits and is true of only two entries, so its slot is better spent on the single most informative ice-cloud cue: fibrous drawn-out edges separate the whole cirrus family, cirrostratus fibratus and the thunderstorm anvil from every rounded water cloud.

why: 4 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: sky_coverage
proposal.question: How much of the sky did it take up?

values.label: one cloud on its own, clear sky all round it
several separate clouds, but more clear sky than cloud
more cloud than sky, but with gaps you could see through
cloud from horizon to horizon, not a gap anywhere

proposal.rationale: Same four bands but defined by the cloud-to-blue ratio rather than vague words, which should stop the isolated/most-of-sky jump; cumulus species are re-assigned to 'several separate clouds' as 80-93% of experts answered.

why: 10 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: single_cloud_outline
proposal.question: If it was one separate cloud, what was its outline?

values.label: it was not one separate cloud - a layer, a veil or many clouds
a smooth almond or saucer, tapering to a point at each end
a long tube of even thickness, like a log lying across the sky
a rounded heap or dome, highest in the middle
a torn shred with no definite outline

proposal.rationale: The lenticularis/volutus mix-ups are the second and eighth largest, and both look like one long cloud; tapered points versus even log thickness is a difference anyone can see at a glance, and the same question isolates every single-cloud entry at once.

why: 1 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: veil_texture
proposal.question: Was the sky covered by a thin whitish veil - one you could still see blue through - and if so, did it have any texture?

values.label: yes, a pale veil with streaks or fibres running through it
yes, a pale veil, completely smooth and featureless
no pale veil - either no layer at all, or a grey sheet that hid the blue

proposal.rationale: Cirrostratus fibratus versus nebulosus is the single biggest mix-up and turns entirely on whether the veil is streaked; asking about it directly, with 'grey sheet that hid the blue' as the third option, also splits cirrostratus from altostratus without needing the sun.

why: 1 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: low_enough_to_touch
proposal.question: Was it low enough to be brushing hilltops, masts or the tops of tall buildings?

values.label: yes - it was down among them, or hiding their tops
no - it was well clear above everything
nothing tall enough in view to judge by

proposal.rationale: Stratus is fog that has not landed, and that is the only thing that reliably separates it from the other featureless grey layers, which between them account for over twenty mix-ups; it needs no instruments, only something tall in sight.

why: 2 values for a person to settle

proposal.name: see_through
proposal.question: Could you see blue sky (or stars) through the body of the cloud itself, rather than through gaps between its parts?

values.label: yes - it was thin enough to see through
no - every part of it was solid to look at

proposal.rationale: Gives the transparency information that the sun question could not supply in three quarters of photos, because it only needs the cloud and the sky behind it; it cleanly lifts the gauzy cirrus and cirrostratus out of every look-alike pairing with solid low cloud.

why: 8 values for a person to settle
